title: Proving the contrapositive
objectives: Prove an implication through its contrapositive, such as “if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even”.

screens.title: Stuck at a square root
screens.prose: Claim: if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even. The table agrees for $n = 1$ to 8. A direct start: $n^2 = 2m$ for an integer $m$, so $n = \sqrt{2m}$.
screens.question: What does $n = \sqrt{2m}$ tell us about whether $n$ is even?

options.text: Nothing useful: $\sqrt{2m}$ shows no factor of 2 we can read off.
$n$ is even, because $2m$ under the root is even.
options.why: You carried evenness through a square root. $\sqrt{8}$ is not even an integer.

options.text: $n = 2\sqrt{m}$, so $n$ is even.
options.why: You took the 2 out of the root. $\sqrt{2m} = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{m}$, not $2\sqrt{m}$.

options.text: $n$ is odd, because roots are rarely whole numbers.
options.why: You guessed from the root. Every even $n^2$ in the table has an even $n$.

hints.text: Try $m = 8$: what is $\sqrt{16}$, and what is $\sqrt{2 \times 8}$ written another way?
A square root does not split into a factor of 2 times an integer.
The direct route gives no form $2k$ for $n$. It is stuck.

feedback.correct: Right. The direct route is stuck at the square root.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether $\sqrt{2m}$ can be written as 2 times an integer.

byKey.out: You moved the 2 outside the root. Only $\sqrt{4m} = 2\sqrt{m}$.

explain.text: Square roots do not keep track of factors of 2. So from $n^2 = 2m$ we cannot write $n = 2k$. We need another way in.

screens.title: Turn it round
screens.prose: From If, then: an implication says the same thing as one of its relatives. The odd rows of the table are highlighted.
screens.question: Which statement says the same as "if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even"?

options.text: If $n$ is odd then $n^2$ is odd.
If $n$ is even then $n^2$ is even.
options.why: You swapped hypothesis and conclusion. That is the converse, a different statement.

options.text: If $n^2$ is odd then $n$ is odd.
options.why: You negated both parts without swapping them. That is the inverse, which agrees with the converse.

options.text: $n^2$ is even and $n$ is odd.
options.why: That is the negation. It says the claim fails.

hints.text: Recall the contrapositive from If, then.
Negate both parts and swap them.
Not $Q$ is "$n$ is odd"; not $P$ is "$n^2$ is odd".

feedback.correct: Right. The contrapositive: if $n$ is odd then $n^2$ is odd.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate both parts, then swap them.

byKey.conv: You swapped the parts but did not negate them. The converse can fail when the original holds.

explain.text: The contrapositive of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$, and it has the same truth table. Its hypothesis, $n$ odd, gives us $n = 2k + 1$. That is a form we can compute with.

screens.title: The proof
screens.prose: **Proof by contrapositive**: to prove $P \Rightarrow Q$, prove $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$ instead. The two are true together, so one proof settles both.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: We prove the contrapositive: if $n$ is odd then $n^2$ is odd.
Suppose $n$ is odd, so $n = 2k + 1$ for an integer $k$.
$2k^2 + 2k$ is an integer, so $n^2$ is odd.
The contrapositive holds, so if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even. $\blacksquare$
Suppose $n$ is even, so $n = 2k$ for an integer $k$.
lines.why: You started from $n$ even. That is the converse's hypothesis, not the contrapositive's.

hints.text: Say first which statement you will prove.
The contrapositive starts from $n$ odd.
Announce; $n = 2k + 1$; square; integer bracket; conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. Announce the contrapositive, prove it directly, then say what it gives.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by naming the contrapositive, then assume $n$ is odd.

byKey.d1: You kept the line assuming $n$ is even. That proves the converse, which is a different claim.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line. The first and last lines say what is proved and why it is enough.

explain.text: We proved "$n$ odd $\Rightarrow$ $n^2$ odd" directly, as in Direct proof. That is the contrapositive of the claim. So the claim holds too.

screens.title: The bracket
screens.prose: The key line of the proof: with $n = 2k + 1$, $n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1$.
screens.question: $4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(\ \square\ ) + 1$. What goes in the bracket?

hints.text: Which terms have a factor 2?
Halve each: $2k^2 + 2k$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the factor 2 out of $4k^2 + 4k$ and leave the 1 outside.

byKey.nohalf: You left $4k^2 + 4k$ as it is. Inside the bracket each term is halved.
byKey.keep1: You moved the 1 inside. It stays outside as the odd part.

explain.text: $4k^2 + 4k = 2(2k^2 + 2k)$, and $2k^2 + 2k$ is an integer. So $n^2$ is 2 times an integer, plus 1. That is the definition of odd.

screens.title: Build the contrapositive
screens.prose: Claim: if $3n + 1$ is even then $n$ is odd. Before proving it, write the statement we will actually prove.
screens.question: Drop a chip into each slot to make the contrapositive. Two chips are not used.

hints.text: Negate both parts of the claim.
Not "$n$ is odd" is "$n$ is even"; not "$3n + 1$ is even" is "$3n + 1$ is odd".
Then swap: if $n$ is even then $3n + 1$ is odd.

feedback.correct: Right. If $n$ is even then $3n + 1$ is odd.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate both parts, then swap them.

byKey.no: You used "$n$ is odd", the claim's own conclusion. The contrapositive negates it.
byKey.te: You used "$3n + 1$ is even", the claim's own hypothesis. It must be negated and moved to the end.
byKey.ne: "$n$ is even" belongs in the If slot.
byKey.to: "$3n + 1$ is odd" belongs in the then slot.

explain.text: The contrapositive is "if $n$ is even then $3n + 1$ is odd". With $n = 2k$, $3n + 1 = 6k + 1 = 2(3k) + 1$, which is odd. The rows $n = 0, 2, 4$ show it: 1, 7 and 13.

screens.title: A harder bracket
screens.prose: Claim: if $n^2 - 6n + 5$ is even then $n$ is odd. We prove the contrapositive: if $n$ is even then $n^2 - 6n + 5$ is odd. Let $n = 2k$, so $n^2 - 6n + 5 = 4k^2 - 12k + 5$.
screens.question: $4k^2 - 12k + 5 = 2(\ \square\ ) + 1$. What goes in the bracket?

hints.text: Split the 5 as $4 + 1$.
Halve each term: $2k^2 - 6k + 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write 5 as $4 + 1$, then take out the factor 2.

byKey.nohalf: You did not halve the terms. Inside the bracket each one is divided by 2.
byKey.five: You put all of the 5 inside. Only 4 of it is even; the 1 stays outside.

explain.text: Writing $5 = 4 + 1$ gives $4k^2 - 12k + 4 + 1 = 2(2k^2 - 6k + 2) + 1$. The bracket is an integer, so the expression is odd. That proves the contrapositive, so the claim holds.

screens.title: The wrong direction
screens.prose: Claim: if $n^2$ is odd then $n$ is odd. Three classmates start a proof.
screens.question: Which opening proves the claim?

options.text: Suppose $n$ is even, so $n = 2k$. Then $n^2 = 2(2k^2)$, which is even.
Suppose $n$ is odd, so $n = 2k + 1$. Then $n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$, which is odd.
options.why: You proved "if $n$ is odd then $n^2$ is odd". That is the converse: true, but a different statement.

options.text: Suppose $n^2$ is even. Then $n$ is even, as we proved.
options.why: You proved "if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even". That is the inverse of this claim, which says the same as its converse.

hints.text: Write the claim as $P \Rightarrow Q$ and name $P$ and $Q$.
$P$ is "$n^2$ is odd" and $Q$ is "$n$ is odd".
The contrapositive starts from not $Q$: $n$ is even.

feedback.correct: Right. Assume $n$ even and show $n^2$ even: the contrapositive.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the opening that starts from the negated conclusion.

byKey.conv: You assumed the conclusion, $n$ odd, and reached the hypothesis. That proves the converse, whatever its algebra.
byKey.inv: You started from $n^2$ even, the negated hypothesis. That proves the inverse, which is the converse in disguise.

explain.text: The claim is $P \Rightarrow Q$ with $P$: $n^2$ odd and $Q$: $n$ odd. Its contrapositive starts from $n$ even and ends at $n^2$ even. The converse is true as well, which is why it tempts, but proving it proves something else.

screens.title: When to turn it round
screens.prose:
$$P \Rightarrow Q \quad \text{says the same as} \quad \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$$

Choose the contrapositive when the hypothesis is about something built from $n$, such as $n^2$ or $3n + 1$. Then the conclusion about $n$ itself becomes the easy starting point.
screens.question: Which pair of results gives $n$ even $\Leftrightarrow$ $n^2$ even?

options.text: Direct: $n = 2k$ gives $n^2 = 2(2k^2)$. Contrapositive: this lesson's proof.
The direct proof twice, once for each direction.
options.why: You used one direction twice. $\Leftrightarrow$ needs $\Rightarrow$ and $\Leftarrow$, two different statements.

options.text: This lesson's proof on its own.
options.why: That gives only "$n^2$ even $\Rightarrow$ $n$ even". The other direction needs its own proof.

options.text: The converse and the inverse of the claim.
options.why: The converse and the inverse say the same thing, so together they give only one direction.

feedback.correct: Right. One direction directly, the other by its contrapositive.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\Leftrightarrow$ needs a proof of each direction.

explain.text: $n$ even $\Rightarrow$ $n^2$ even is a one-line direct proof. $n^2$ even $\Rightarrow$ $n$ even needed the contrapositive. Together they give $n$ even $\Leftrightarrow$ $n^2$ even, which the next lesson uses.

screens.title: Not always
screens.prose: Claim: if $n$ is even then $n + 2$ is even. Both methods work here.
screens.question: Which proof is shorter?

options.text: Direct: $n = 2k$, so $n + 2 = 2(k + 1)$.
Contrapositive: suppose $n + 2$ is odd, and show $n$ is odd.
options.why: That works, but $n + 2 = 2m + 1$ gives $n = 2(m - 1) + 1$. It is an extra rearranging step.

options.text: They are equally long, so the choice never matters.
options.why: You assumed the methods cost the same. Here the hypothesis gives $n = 2k$ at once, so the direct proof is shorter.

hints.text: Is the hypothesis already about $n$ itself?
"$n$ is even" gives $n = 2k$ straight away.

feedback.correct: Right. When the hypothesis is about $n$ itself, a direct proof is usually shortest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the steps each method needs.

explain.text: The hypothesis already gives $n = 2k$, so $n + 2 = 2(k + 1)$ in one line. The contrapositive needs a rearrangement first. Choosing the method is part of the work.

screens.title: A two-position book
screens.prose: A book holds two positions. Its risk rule: "if the book loses more than £100 today, at least one position lost more than £50." Negating "at least one" needs care.
screens.question: Drop a chip into each slot to make the contrapositive. Three chips are not used.

tokens.text: at least one position lost more than £50
at least one position lost at most £50

hints.text: Negate the conclusion first.
The opposite of "at least one lost more than £50" is "each lost at most £50".
If each position lost at most £50, then the book lost at most £100.

feedback.correct: Right. If each position lost at most £50, the book lost at most £100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate both parts, then swap them.

byKey.slip: You kept "at least one". As in Saying the opposite, not "some lost more" is "each lost at most".
byKey.ph: You used the rule's own hypothesis. The contrapositive negates it and moves it to the end.
byKey.pc: You used the rule's own conclusion. The contrapositive starts from its negation.
byKey.h: "each position lost at most £50" belongs in the If slot.
byKey.c: "the book lost at most £100" belongs in the then slot.

explain.text: Not "some position lost more than £50" is "every position lost at most £50". Not "the book lost more than £100" is "the book lost at most £100". The contrapositive joins them, and adding the two inequalities proves it.

screens.title: The written proof
screens.prose: Now the proof a risk committee could check.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: We prove the contrapositive. Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be the two losses in £.
So the book lost at most £100, and by the contrapositive the rule holds. $\blacksquare$
Suppose the book lost £120. Then one position lost at least £60.
lines.why: You worked one day's numbers. The proof must cover every pair of losses.

hints.text: Announce the method and name the losses.
Assume the contrapositive's hypothesis.
Name; assume both at most 50; add; conclude.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the losses, assume each is at most £50, then add.

byKey.d1: You kept the example with £120. One day's numbers cannot cover every day.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Two inequalities in the same direction can be added: $L_1 \le 50$ and $L_2 \le 50$ give $L_1 + L_2 \le 100$. That is the contrapositive. So a loss over £100 forces some position over £50.

ideas: $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$ are true together, so proving the contrapositive proves the claim.
Turn a claim round when its hypothesis is about something built from $n$ and its conclusion is about $n$.
Negate both parts with care: not "at least one" is "every", and not "or" is "and".

formula.name: Contrapositive
formula.note: Negate both parts and swap them.

summary.trap: Proving the converse, $Q \Rightarrow P$, proves a different statement, even when the converse is true.

options.text: If $a < 50$ and $b < 50$ then $a + b < 100$.
If $a < 50$ or $b < 50$ then $a + b < 100$.
options.why: You negated each part but kept "or". Negating an "or" gives an "and".

options.text: If $a \ge 50$ or $b \ge 50$ then $a + b \ge 100$.
options.why: You swapped the parts without negating them. That is the converse.

options.text: If $a + b < 100$ then $a < 50$ and $b < 50$.
options.why: You negated without swapping. That is the inverse.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate the conclusion with De Morgan, then swap.

explain.text: By De Morgan, not ($a \ge 50$ or $b \ge 50$) is $a < 50$ and $b < 50$. That becomes the hypothesis, and $a + b < 100$ the conclusion. Adding $a < 50$ and $b < 50$ proves it.

quiz.prose: "Suppose $n$ is even, so $n = 2k$. Then $3n + 1 = 2(3k) + 1$ is odd. So if $3n + 1$ is even then $n$ is odd. $\blacksquare$"
quiz.question: Which method does this proof use?

options.text: Proof by contrapositive
Direct proof of the claim
options.why: You read the algebra as direct. It starts from not-the-conclusion, $n$ even, so it proves the contrapositive.

options.text: A proof of the converse
options.why: The converse would start from $n$ odd. This proof starts from $n$ even.

options.text: Checking an example
options.why: No example is checked: $k$ is any integer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the proof's first line with the claim's conclusion.

explain.text: The claim is "$3n + 1$ even $\Rightarrow$ $n$ odd". The proof starts from $n$ even, the negated conclusion, and reaches $3n + 1$ odd. That is the contrapositive.

quiz.prose: Claim: if $7n + 4$ is even then $n$ is even. Contrapositive: suppose $n = 2k + 1$, so $7n + 4 = 14k + 11$.
quiz.question: $14k + 11 = 2(\ \square\ ) + 1$. What goes in the bracket?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write 11 as $10 + 1$, then take out the factor 2.

byKey.eleven: You kept all of 11 inside. Only 10 of it is even.
byKey.nohalf: You did not halve the terms inside the bracket.

explain.text: $14k + 11 = 14k + 10 + 1 = 2(7k + 5) + 1$. So $n$ odd gives $7n + 4$ odd. That is the contrapositive, so the claim holds.

quiz.prose: Claim: if $n^3$ is even then $n$ is even.
quiz.question: Which approach is easiest?

options.text: Prove that if $n$ is odd then $n^3$ is odd.
Write $n^3 = 2m$, so $n = \sqrt[3]{2m}$.
options.why: You took the direct route. A cube root, like a square root, shows no factor of 2.

options.text: Prove that if $n$ is even then $n^3$ is even.
options.why: That is the converse. It is true, but it proves a different statement.

options.text: Check $n = 1$ to 10.
options.why: Checking cases is evidence. It covers ten integers, not all of them.

feedback.correct: Right. The hypothesis is about $n^3$, built from $n$, so turn it round.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which statement starts from something about $n$ itself.

explain.text: With $n = 2k + 1$, $n^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1 = 2(4k^3 + 6k^2 + 3k) + 1$, which is odd. That proves the contrapositive. A cube root would leave us stuck, as the square root did.
